storm.summary_layperson: A line of afternoon storms tied to a cold front is passing just west of the cove right now and pulling away to the east, and while the front itself should clear the area by early evening, forecasters are still flagging a chance of an isolated strong storm or heavy downpour into the early evening.
storm.local_effect_blurb: Sound water (76°F) is only about 2–3°F cooler than the air, far short of the gap needed for the cove to meaningfully weaken or block incoming storms.
storm.detail_html:
A cold front is sweeping through the area this afternoon, and radar (KOKX) shows exactly that happening right now: a cluster of cells within 2–3 miles of the cove itself, topping out at 54 dBZ — real, fairly vigorous precipitation, not clutter. The good news is the cluster is largely departing: most cells are tracked as moving away to the north/northeast or sitting quasi-stationary just west of the cove, with the broader reflectivity field drifting east at about 15 kt. None of the tracked cells are currently classified as closing on the cove, so there's no fresh ETA to quote for this window.

The Sound isn't offering any protection today. Water is 76°F against air near 79°F — only a 2–3°F gap, far below the roughly 10°F delta this pipeline treats as the threshold for a real marine-layer choke. protective_mechanism_active reads false, so call the local effect neutral: the cove will see whatever the regional picture serves up, with no Sound-driven discount or amplification. Deep-layer shear is a healthy 33–34 kt from the SW, which is enough to organize storms but just under the 35 kt this pipeline treats as the amplification trigger, and there's no active sea breeze in play today to interact with it anyway.

The bigger caveat for the 17:00–22:00 window: HRRR's own instability forecast actually ticks CAPE up to about 1800 J/kg right at 17:00 before collapsing to near zero by 19:00 as the front clears out, and the NWS Area Forecast Discussion explicitly calls out an “isolated severe and flash flood threat” each afternoon/early evening this week, plus a chance of brief NW gusts 25–35 mph right behind the frontal passage. So the most likely story is a narrowing window of residual shower/storm risk in the first hour or so after 17:00, transitioning to clearing, gusty post-frontal conditions for the rest of the evening.

What would push this to high: a new cell developing nearby and tracked as closing on the cove, or NWS issuing a severe thunderstorm/flash flood warning — worth a radar check right around 17:00–18:00 given the CAPE bump. No alerts are active as of this writing.

wind.tactics_blurb: Moderate gradient wind, not a sea-breeze day — starts SW around 9 kt and veers hard to W/WNW as a cold front crosses mid-window, holding 6–9 kt through 10 PM rather than dying. Favor the middle of the course once it settles into W/WNW; expect a persistent shift, not oscillations.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
This is a gradient-only day (B-moderate): the air–water temperature gap is only 2.5°F, well short of the 5°F needed to build a real sea breeze, so today's wind is entirely synoptic — driven by the cold front crossing the area this afternoon, not by heating. The well-sited station average is right at 10 kt, which lands this squarely in the moderate gradient bucket rather than light or strong.

Riverside YC's own anemometer is currently reading W at just 2.7 kt with a 22 kt gust and a 10-minute average near 11 kt — a big divergence (about 51°) from the regional ensemble median of SW 224°. That's not a cove-specific eddy; it's the passing storm cluster sitting almost on top of the station right now. Treat the current RYC read as storm-contaminated rather than representative, and lean on the HRRR trend plus the regional ensemble for the forecast hours instead.

The window's real story is the frontal veer: HRRR has the wind starting SW (~225°) at 17:00, swinging through W by 18:00, and settling into WNW (285–300°) for the back half of the window as the front clears out. That's a persistent shift — commit to the new direction as it arrives rather than playing it as an oscillation. Per the cove geography table, SW flow is fairly even across the course with a slight edge to the east/mouth side; once it's W–WNW, expect more holes near the CT shore and better average pressure mid-cove, which is why the center favors both halves of the window on balance.

Speed holds in the 6–9 kt range all evening — no sunset collapse to worry about since this is gradient-driven, not thermal — squarely in one-design dinghy territory, a bit soft in the 19:00–20:00 lull as the front finishes crossing, then picking back up slightly by 21:00. The 22:00 row leans on HRRR's lower-confidence extended outlook rather than the primary hourly forecast, so treat that last hour as a rough continuation of the WNW trend rather than a precise call.
